It is about having meaningful choices cooperating from a position of confidence, and ensuring that our digital assets remain secure, resilient, interoperable, and aligned with our democratic values. This is why the European Commission has proposed its Tech Sovereignty package, including the EU Open Digital Ecosystem strategy. That's our new open source strategy. Today, I would like to focus on one key objective: objective: promoting open and interoperable digital ecosystems for public administrations as a foundation for strategic independence across all layers of governance. For the European Commission, we have developed a practical framework that others may wish to draw on. Digital sovereignty cannot be achieved through a single technology choice or one-off decision. It must be embedded in how public administrations design, procure, operate, and maintain digital systems. Our framework rests on three pillars: trusted digital assets that are secure, reliable, and reusable; capabilities and communities to sustain them over time; and governance that keeps technology choices aligned with long-term public interests. Together, these pillars support digital ecosystems that are both technically sound and institutionally sustainable. But open digital ecosystems are not only about software. They are also about capacity, stewardship, and avoiding future dependencies through today's decisions. Public authorities should not only be users of technology, They should also be contributors, partners, and co-creators of the systems on which they depend. This transition requires trusted partnerships and collaboration across borders. In Europe, we are already putting these foundations in place. My services facilitate a growing EU Ospol network, bringing together public administrations to exchange practices align approaches, and strengthen capacity around the sustainable use and governance of open source. We are also investing in shared digital assets. The EU Open Source Solutions Catalogue helps administrations discover and reuse public sector open source solutions, reducing duplication and accelerating innovation. New forms of cooperation are also emerging, Through initiatives such as the EDICS, that's the European Digital Infrastructure Consortium, we have the Digital Commons EDIC and the Impact EDIC, where member states are pooling resources and expertise to jointly develop interoperable digital capabilities and strengthen collective resilience. This ecosystem approach also connects to the Commission's broader technological sovereignty agenda. Through initiatives such as the forthcoming Cloud and AI Development Act, or CAADA, we aim to strengthen resilience in strategic digital infrastructure while preserving meaningful choices and reducing excessive dependencies. The Commission is also seeking to lead by example. Earlier this year, we introduced sovereignty requirements into a major sovereign cloud procurement for EU institutions. And we developed a sovereign cloud framework to help organizations assess and strengthen digital resilience. Europe's strength in the digital age does not lie in going alone. It lies in collective action. And this spirit of cooperation extends well beyond Europe's borders. Through the UN ITU Open Source Ecosystem Enabler Initiative, supported by the European Union, We are helping to establish open source program offices beyond Europe, including in Trinidad and Tobago, where early successes already demonstrate the value of open collaboration in strengthening digital capabilities. Let me conclude with one final thought. Strategic independence is not a challenge for one institution, one level of government, or one region alone. It is a shared responsibility across the public sector, from cities and regions to national governments and international organizations. The technologies on which we depend are becoming more interconnected and essential to our societies. This makes cooperation not simply desirable, but necessary. Strategic independence should therefore not be understood as standing apart, It is the ability to cooperate from a position of confidence, with meaningful choices and shared stewardship over the digital foundations on which our public services, economies and democracies increasingly depend. Thank you very much.

Thanks very much. It's a pleasure to be here, an honor actually. And so in this guardian role, I think about kind of where we come from, where we're going, and this notion of taking stock, to me this is a social movement. It just happens to produce technology, which is why it's irreversible. There's an inevitability about participation, whether you are a country, whether you are a company, public sector, private sector, there's a movement that's inexorable toward collaborative development, which is one of the critical components and tenets of open source. We collaborate to compete more effectively. We don't think about— the first thing we think about is not to solve it independently, but we think about what are the ways that I can build on someone else's ideas that have already been established. And what it takes is a certain level of humility. And this is something that all of us need to practice in the community. We always need to step back and think about how we can be better by distilling the collective intelligence of a population of people around the world, not just around our company or around our neighborhood if we're in Silicon Valley or Route 128, or if we're in Sophi Antipolis or wherever else in the world. We are collaborating and we are Through the process of collaboration, we have engaged and incited a group of people, the Open Source Program Office Directors, that have carried the message, have done so many different things to be able to advance the message inside companies, inside governments, to be able to awaken people to the notion of value and how value is created in the new economy. We are— I think the concept was developed— Brian Arthur, an economist, commented on Ken Arrow's work on increasing returns about 18 years ago in an article that stuck with me. And when I got into open source 19 years ago, it made me kind of think about the whole idea of 1 1 1 doesn't equal 3. It equals 6 or 10 or 20 when we bring smart people together and allow them to solve problems in software. This is a critical component of value that every day we are involved in. Every day we see people communicating with each other. CEOs have no idea who their team members are communicating with, how they're communicating, what they're communicating. They only know that by having this unbridled capacity to collaborate, we are doing things that we couldn't do and we are innovating. What the— there are lots of articles that have been written over the years, but Clayton Christensen probably at Harvard was one of the best oracles of this message that we bring the outside in to be able to enrich our environments and our organizations so that we can bring new ideas in. We see time and time again acquisitions of new companies don't get it done. Joint ventures don't get it done. Multi-party collaborations don't get it done. But open source does get it done. It increases the level of innovation that we are able to, to, to access, and it changes the way we create value in the new economy. And OSPOs are a key component that people— I've seen them evolve over these 19 years, and I've seen The Japanese team that was up was talking about— they're the next generation of OSPOs, because I can remember when Fujitsu founded the first open source program office director position in Japan, probably about 20 years ago. It was right before I arrived on the scene, and I thought about how this role has evolved in preparation for these making these preliminary comments, and I see that the increased kind of importance of these individuals and the role that they play, with humility— they're not the, you know, just like I think, you know, Jim Zemlin spoke to you earlier, Mike Malinkovich will speak to you in a little while on the panel. These are people who are doing really significant things to be able to create what I'll call project-based innovation, which is the most powerful force for innovation in the world right now. We get together in projects, we have talented people that are managing these projects that we bring in, that develop processes and procedures to be able to allow people to come together and to be able to create something that would not be available or accessible without this notion of collaboration that's so central. And so you think about the idea of their— Ospos are translators. They take a message and they translate it. They help provide kind of a conversion of raw ideas and concepts and make it saleable, make it palatable to individuals that are potentially leaders of companies, CTOs, deputy CTOs, heads of software, and other individuals, not only in their own companies, but across the industries that they participate in. They're oracles in their own way of the message of how powerful open source is. And then, you know, they're communicators. We have an obligation to participate in a certain way. We have an obligation to lift each other up. It's not Fujitsu competing against Hitachi. It's about both companies raising each other up with processes and procedures that help us to be able to redefine what innovation is and to accelerate the capacity for innovation that only open source unlocks. They're advocates. Very often they've had to fight inside companies, particularly early on in the history of open source, to be able to have people become aware of the importance of this movement that is open source. Many people in senior positions inside companies get to some extent of it, but they don't get it all. They don't truly understand the power of open source as I'm describing it and as I understand it. They're educators. They're not just communicating a message and establishing norms and a sense of who we are and how we participate and what the expectations are in this community. There's a special Again, the special sense of learnership that I find and I found from the beginning in these individuals who are connectors. We can all be understanding the power of open source as a social movement that produces innovation that is of incredible significance and import to all of us in every sector and every industry where we find software. so we believe that open source, with its transparency, reusability, local adaptation, and continuous improvement, and that the various communities and all the different groups provide to continue to keep it up to date and even more robust potentially than some of the other vendor-provided platform, this is really a great opportunity for many countries, especially developing countries, who may not have the economic means to be able to purchase those products and platforms that are provided by some of the few global companies that can potentially be locked into. And to be able to continue to leverage and evolve it, leveraging a larger community of people that are supporting the various platforms around the AI and not being, again, locked into a specific product company or a specific country or vendor that the product is being developed from. It's not the product or technology that makes the decision, but it's really the government who needs to own it. So make sure that the government has the institutional capability to monitor and intervene as needed and be able to challenge the decision the AI is making and being able to really responsibly using the AI. And this is is, you know, goes back to the responsible use of AI, is such a critical, important aspect of how we're leveraging this and giving more independence to the various governments who's adapting it and really leveraging it well. Thank you.

Um, I— when it comes to how AI is going to impact government, I, I want to actually take a very different and quite specific point of view, um, which is around the topic of security, uh, cybersecurity specifically. So governments all have digital services. They have basically— governments have basically become the IT department of the nation. Prepare to get your ass kicked. The— there's— more than one thing can be true at the same time. So Project Glasswing was an excellent marketing campaign by Anthropic. It was really well executed. It's also true that, um, Mythos is a very powerful model that delivers, um, lots of vulnerabilities. More worryingly, um, what it does is it actually delivers a playbook, an attack playbook. So it's not just, "Here's your vulnerability." It's like, "And here's how you exploit it and here's the script." Um, it's going to be messy, uh, and every IT department, uh, of which governments are one, need to fundamentally change the way that they think about their running systems. If you are not prepared to repatch and reboot every server in your infrastructure several times a day, you're going to be in trouble. And so, and that's a huge cultural change. Every IT— I mean, I've been in IT. Every IT department in the planet, like, you— and, you know, you put it up, you stand it up if it's work, If it ain't broke, don't fix it. Right? And they just run this. I remember talking to like one of my own IT guys, like bragging about the fact that he hadn't rebooted a server in 9 years. Hmm, excellent. But that's, and that has been the perception of IT departments for as long as there have been IT departments. And fundamentally that's going to change. And I think that we really have to think as governments, you have to start really thinking about how you are going to change the culture and the security posture in your IT departments to be relentlessly using AI on the defense. It's not because then there— because there are definitely ways to do that. Again, to Brian's point, you have to have the right harnesses, you have to know how to use the right prompts, you have to train your people to do this, but you need to start really using AI to automate your cyber defense.
